newsitem.title: FRANCE: Feature - Urban diet helps solve Iran wheat import mystery.
newsitem.headline: Feature - Urban diet helps solve Iran wheat import mystery.

text.p: Grain traders and officials think they have an answer to the riddle of massive Iranian wheat purchases that caught the West completely off guard this year.

It may not be the most dramatic theory sparked by recent earthquakes and rumours of clandestine trade with neighbours, but traders are convinced Iran is quietly buying wheat to catch up with rapid growth in its own cities and bake better bread.
Other temporary factors may have expanded the bubble, but many now see it as a major importer in grain for years to come.
Iran jumped from relative obscurity as an importer to become the world's largest wheat buyer in the space of a few months, sending shock signals through foreign embassies and trade firms.
The United States was first to highlight the full extent of imports in April but admitted it could not explain it. Others talked of widespread smuggling out of Iran or wasted crops.
"Nobody really knows why they're buying so much," a senior U.S. agriculture official said in Washington earlier this month.

The London-based International Grains Council, an authoritative market monitor, estimated Iran's imports at 6.6 million tonnes in the year to June 30. But its May 1 survey also failed to shed light on why imports had doubled in one year.
Analysts speculated much of the grain was slipping over Iran's borders with Central Asia including to war-racked Afghanistan -- seen as a rich target for smugglers.
PRICES ROCKET
Flour prices rocketed in Kabul after Pakistan closed its own border with Afghanistan on March 29 to check wheat shortages.
But while smuggling may exist, traders say it explains no more than a fraction of the extra three million tonnes imported.
"It's a lot of wheat. You can't just hide it," one said.
Other potential customers like Turkmenistan to the north can buy wheat more cheaply from neighbouring Kazakhstan.
A series of powerful earthquakes culminating in a devastating tremor in eastern Iran earlier this month may have sped up the buying, but for now wheat crops seem largely spared, traders said.
So, suppliers increasingly reckon the main answer for Iran's soaring demand must lie in its domestic situation.
Changes in urban demand and new storage are likely to keep demand buoyant, if not quite as high, for some time, they say.

"Consumption is rapidly rising on a regular basis and more people are moving from rice ... consumption to wheat," a Western trader who closely monitors the region said. "It's growing demand and growing population and also changes in diet."
The same problem is shared by other big importers from Cairo to China -- how to feed mushrooming urban populations at a time when diets are changing to include greater reliance on grain.
But in Iran's case, disappointment with the quality of its crop, rather than its size, has forced it to import even more to improve the bread supply to its packed cities, analysts said.
"The imported wheat basically goes for urban consumption to complement the local harvest," another commodity trader said.
United Nations figures show 59 percent of Iranians lived in cities in 1994, a figure expected to reach 75 percent by 2025.
Iran, which subsidises bread for its 65 million people, has industrialised baking in recent years to keep up with demand.
But it has been difficult to ensure the quality of the long, flat loaf Iranians traditionally prefer by using local wheat, a specialist on Iranian grain based outside the country said.
Some of the rejected wheat is fed to animals, he added.
IRANIAN PASTA

A modest but rapidly growing Iranian pasta industry may have contributed to imports of special durum wheat from Canada this year -- up to 600,000 tonnes, according to traders. Durum can also can be blended with other grades to boost quality.

Keeping pace with such demand has become a hot issue both at home and abroad. While Iran diverts extra hard currency into wheat, its suppliers led by Australia have been trying to smooth over last month's international row over a Berlin court ruling implicating Iranian leaders in political murders in Germany.
That ruling, denounced by Tehran, raised fears of a new crisis in Iran's trade relations worldwide, though concerns about a big drop in grain traffic have not materialised.
Current suppliers include Canada, Argentina and the European Union, whose ties with Tehran had been most directly at risk.
Some analysts speculate imports received priority earlier this year as an insurance policy against a worse diplomatic fall-out from the April 10 court verdict than actually happened.
Another reason to play safe with imports may have been the run-up to May 23 presidential elections, they said, noting Iran now had more wheat silos to store away purchases.
But such a policy also has some risks. The import surge has fuelled implied criticism in Iran's press, with the influential Tehran Times demanding "proper reasons" to justify it.
The English-language paper warned overdependence on foreign nations for staple foods could "even lead to a political crisis in the country, threatening the whole Islamic system".

Iran's wheat purchases are worth an estimated $1 billion at today's prices. But by acting early and mostly in secret, its buyers probably escaped the brunt of a 15 percent rise in dollar-denominated world prices since January, traders said.
IMPORTS COULD SLOW
Depending on how the next crop appears, imports could lose steam temporarily as silos start to fill up, traders said.
A late winter and lack of water caused some crop losses but ample rain arrived in February and the picture is looking up.

The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) predicts an average Iranian wheat crop of about 10 million tonnes, down two percent from last year. The new harvest, mainly grown in the north and west, is just starting to be stored.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani told the Majlis assembly in December that Iran planned to build seven new silos able to store 451,000 tonnes of wheat in the year from March 21, 1997.
Officials also believe a closer look at the timing of deliveries will help sort out the real trend in consumption -- rising, but not quite as wildly as diplomats first assumed.
The Rome-based FAO believes up to a million tonnes of the wheat bought abroad since last summer might only reach Iran after the harvest and should be counted as next year's demand.

That aside, the message from Iran's big cities is that it will not fade from the world market any time soon, traders said. Most put next year's imports between 4.6 and 7.0 million tonnes -- a wide range but firmly above recent averages of 3.5 million.
Higher projected oil revenues may help absorb the cost but financing is expected to remain a sensitive issue, they said.
